description: The infinite product over primes ∏_p (1-p⁻²)⁻¹ equals π²/6, connecting the Basel sum to prime numbers via Euler's product formula.

overview.historicalContext:
Euler made two groundbreaking discoveries about infinite series in the 1730s. In 1734, he solved the Basel Problem (posed by Pietro Mengoli in 1644 and unsolved for ~90 years): ∑_{n=1}^∞ 1/n² = π²/6. His proof used the infinite product factorization of sin(πx)/πx, a technique that was later made rigorous by Weierstrass. The Basel result connected the sum of reciprocal squares — a purely arithmetic object — to π, which was deeply surprising to contemporaries.

In 1737, Euler discovered the product representation ζ(s) = ∏_p (1-p⁻ˢ)⁻¹, where the product runs over all prime numbers. The key insight was to expand each factor as a geometric series: (1-p⁻ˢ)⁻¹ = 1 + p⁻ˢ + p⁻²ˢ + ..., then observe that multiplying over all primes generates exactly the terms n⁻ˢ for all natural numbers n, by the fundamental theorem of arithmetic (unique prime factorization).

Combining these two results at s=2 gives ∏_p (1-p⁻²)⁻¹ = π²/6, connecting the distribution of primes to π. The reciprocal ∏_p (1-1/p²) = 6/π² ≈ 0.6079 has a beautiful probabilistic interpretation (Cesàro 1881): it equals the probability that two randomly chosen positive integers are coprime. This formalization captures all three equivalent forms (tprod, HasProd, Tendsto) of this identity using Mathlib's `riemannZeta_eulerProduct` family and `riemannZeta_two`.
overview.problemStatement: Prove that the infinite product ∏_p (1-p⁻²)⁻¹ over all primes p equals π²/6.
overview.text: The Euler product form of the Basel Problem: ∏_p (1-p⁻²)⁻¹ = π²/6.
overview.proofStrategy:
Direct combination of two Mathlib theorems:
1. riemannZeta_eulerProduct_tprod: ∏_p (1-p^{-s})⁻¹ = ζ(s) for Re(s) > 1
2. riemannZeta_two: ζ(2) = π²/6

Substituting s = 2 and chaining the equalities gives the result.
keyInsights: The proof is a 2-line combination of existing Mathlib infrastructure — the power of formal libraries.
Three equivalent formulations capture different aspects: tprod (value), HasProd (convergence proof), Tendsto (partial product convergence).
The identity ∏_p (1-1/p²) = 6/π² ≈ 0.6079 gives the density of coprime pairs among integers.
Euler's original argument expanded each (1-p⁻ˢ)⁻¹ as a geometric series and used unique factorization.

The condition Re(s) > 1 is essential for convergence: at s=1 the product diverges (harmonic series), reflecting the infinitude of primes. The Euler product is the key analytic tool connecting the multiplicative structure of integers (primes) to additive structure (sums). The Riemann hypothesis is essentially a question about the zeros of this product as a function of complex s.

sections.title: The Main Theorem: Euler Product at s=2
sections.summary: The Euler product ∏_p (1-p⁻²)⁻¹ = π²/6 in three equivalent forms: tprod (value), HasProd (convergence proof), Tendsto (partial product limit).
sections.mathContext: $\prod_p (1-p^{-2})^{-1} = \zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$. Three Lean formulations: `tprod` gives the value; `HasProd` gives a convergence proof; `Tendsto` shows partial products converge.

sections.title: Convergence Condition: Re(2) > 1
sections.summary: The helper two_re_gt_one proves Re(2) > 1, satisfying the convergence hypothesis for riemannZeta_eulerProduct_tprod.
sections.mathContext: $\text{Re}(2) = 2 > 1$ ensures the Euler product $\prod_p(1-p^{-s})^{-1}$ converges absolutely. At $\text{Re}(s) = 1$ (e.g., $s = 1$) the product diverges, reflecting $\sum 1/p = \infty$.

sections.title: The Basel Sum ∑ 1/n² = π²/6
sections.summary: The Basel sum ∑ 1/n² = π²/6 in HasSum form, connecting the arithmetic series to the Euler product via ζ(2).

sections.title: Euler's 1737 Geometric Series Argument
sections.summary: Explains Euler's derivation using geometric series expansion and unique prime factorization to connect ζ(s) to the product over primes.
sections.mathContext: $(1-p^{-s})^{-1} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} p^{-ks}$. Multiplying over all primes gives $\prod_p (1-p^{-s})^{-1} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{-s}$ by unique factorization.

sections.title: Probabilistic Interpretation: Coprimality Density
sections.summary: The reciprocal ∏_p(1-1/p²) = 6/π² ≈ 0.6079 equals the probability that two randomly chosen positive integers are coprime (Cesàro 1881).
sections.mathContext: $\Pr[\gcd(m,n)=1] = \prod_p (1 - 1/p^2) = 6/\pi^2 \approx 0.6079$. Each prime $p$ independently avoids dividing both integers with probability $1-1/p^2$.

conclusion.summary: A fully verified proof that ∏_p (1-p⁻²)⁻¹ = π²/6, combining the Euler product formula with the Basel identity. Zero axioms, zero sorries. The proof is a 2-line combination of Mathlib's riemannZeta_eulerProduct_tprod and riemannZeta_two.
openQuestions: Can the Euler product be extended to Dirichlet L-functions L(s,χ) = ∏_p (1-χ(p)p⁻ˢ)⁻¹ for Dirichlet characters χ in Lean, using Mathlib's existing Dirichlet series infrastructure?
Can the prime number theorem be formally derived from the analytic properties of the Euler product (specifically, the non-vanishing of ζ(s) on Re(s)=1) using Mathlib's complex analysis?
Can the probabilistic statement Pr[gcd(m,n)=1] = 6/π² be formalized using Mathlib's measure theory for the natural density of coprime pairs?
conclusion.implications: Connects Euler's product formula to the Riemann zeta function, establishing a foundational bridge between analytic and algebraic number theory. The three Lean formulations (tprod, HasProd, Tendsto) show Mathlib's maturity in handling infinite products over primes.

crossReferences.description: Companion entry formalizing the Euler product ∏_p (1-p⁻ˢ)⁻¹ = ζ(s) via the geometric series expansion (1-p⁻ˢ)⁻¹ = ∑_k p⁻ˢᵏ and unique factorization — the same mathematical argument underlying this proof.
Unique prime factorization is the key ingredient enabling Euler's product identity: every integer has a unique factorization, so ∏_p ∑_k p⁻ˢᵏ = ∑_n n⁻ˢ with each n appearing exactly once.
Dirichlet's theorem on primes in progressions uses L-functions L(s,χ) = ∏_p (1-χ(p)p⁻ˢ)⁻¹ — the direct generalization of the Euler product twisted by a Dirichlet character χ.

At s=1, the Euler product ∏_p (1-p⁻¹)⁻¹ = ζ(1) diverges (harmonic series), establishing ∑ 1/p = ∞ and proving infinitely many primes. The current proof at s=2 is the convergent counterpart, where the product value π²/6 encodes the coprimality density 6/π².

Euler's totient product formula φ(n)/n = ∏_{p|n} (1-1/p) is a finite multiplicative analogue of the Euler product. The infinite product ∏_p (1-1/p²) = 6/π² appearing here is the probabilistic form of the same multiplicative structure.
